To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the presence of a Schwann cell-like phenotype in human neuroblastoma clones is associated with the secretion of collagen, which is a major constituent of the extracellular matrix of Schwann cells and of other glial cells.
human neuroblastoma clones with different morphology synthesize different amounts of collagen and that this is associated with differences in the expression of the pro-alpha 2(I) gene.
the proportion of cells that are substrate-adherent and large correlates with the amount of collagen produced by human neuroblastomas.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the differentiation of neuroblastoma cells in vitro.
the characterization of the two morphologically distinct cell types present in cultures of human tumors derived from the neural crest.
the study of the differentiation of human neuroblastomas in cell culture.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neuroblastoma is a neuroectodermal tumor that is capable of differentiating into Schwann cells, and that the presence of Schwann cells in neuroblastomas is not a result of Schwann cell invasion.
the S-type cells are glial cells and the N-type cells are neuronal.
the S-type cells are glial cells of Schwann cell origin.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neuroblastoma cell is a multipotential neural crest-derived cell that has the capacity to differentiate into both neural and non-neural cell types.
the S-type cells are Schwann cells.
the presence of the S-type cells in human neuroblastoma cultures is due to a differentiation of the neuroblast-like cells into glial-type cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of large, substrate-attached cells in neuroblast cultures is a good indicator that the cells are differentiating.
the S-type cells are the ones that produce collagen, and the S-type cells can be differentiated into glial cells.
human neuroblastoma cultures can serve as a useful model to study the mechanisms of glial differentiation.
